name: CLadder
summary: 10,112 yes-or-no questions that ask for formal causal inference, from probabilities to counterfactuals, about small described worlds whose causal structure is stated.
overview:
CLadder tests whether a language model can carry out formal causal inference stated in words. Each question describes a small, self-contained hypothetical world: which variables directly affect which, and a few probabilities, such as how often people who drink clean water get cholera. It then asks a yes-or-no question whose answer follows from the rules of causal inference. Zhijing Jin, Yuen Chen, Felix Leeb, Luigi Gresele, and colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, ETH Zürich, and other institutions presented it at NeurIPS 2023. They built it because earlier evaluations of causality in language models mostly tested commonsense causal knowledge, and a model can pass those by repeating causal claims from its training text without reasoning about them. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04350)

The questions are generated, not written. A generator picks a causal graph, such as a chain, a fork, a confounder, a mediator, an instrumental variable, or a front-door structure, and a query from one of the three rungs of Judea Pearl's Ladder of Causation. Rung 1 asks about association, such as marginal and conditional probabilities. Rung 2 asks about interventions, such as the average treatment effect or which variables form a valid adjustment set. Rung 3 asks about counterfactuals, such as the effect of treatment on the treated or natural direct and indirect effects. The generator draws probabilities for which the answer can be identified, computes the answer and a step-by-step derivation with a causal inference engine, and then turns the variables into a story from templates. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04350)

Stories come in three kinds. Commonsensical stories follow examples from the causality literature, such as smoking and lung cancer or a vaccine and smallpox. Anti-commonsensical stories replace the treatment or the outcome with an unrelated variable. Nonsensical stories replace every variable with a random four-letter word. Because the stated probabilities decide the answer, a model that answers from world knowledge goes wrong on the last two kinds while formal reasoning still succeeds. [README](https://github.com/causalNLP/cladder/blob/3d2d1169b4b939a09048a6a75956c8972a93cc38/README.md) and [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04350)

In the paper's results on this set, GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) answered 62.03% of the questions correctly and GPT-3.5 52.18%, against 49.27% for random guessing. The authors' CausalCoT prompt, which walks the model through extracting the graph, classifying and formalizing the query, gathering the data, deriving the estimand, and calculating it, raised GPT-4 to 70.40%: 83.35% on rung 1, 67.47% on rung 2, and 62.05% on rung 3. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04350)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete balanced set, `cladder-v1-q-balanced.json`, read from the archive `data/cladder-v1.zip` at commit `3d2d116` of causalNLP/cladder: 10,112 questions, of which 3,160 are on rung 1, 3,160 on rung 2, and 3,792 on rung 3, with 5,056 answered yes and 5,056 no. The paper names the balanced set as the main benchmark of CLadder v1.5. It was added to the archive on 2023-08-03, beside files that keep the name v1; the archive has not changed since, and the importer checks its SHA-256 digest. The other files in the archive, including the aggregate set that was the main benchmark of v1.0 and the easy, hard, commonsense, anti-commonsense, and nonsense variants, are not imported. The authors' Hugging Face copy, whose default split is labelled v1.5, holds the same 10,112 question numbers with the same answers and prompts. [Repository](https://github.com/causalNLP/cladder/tree/3d2d1169b4b939a09048a6a75956c8972a93cc38), [Hugging Face copy](https://huggingface.co/datasets/causal-nlp/CLadder/tree/18d684e444ed07cc57ae0f3a91ee983a79b8119a), and [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04350)

Each Task Prompt is the prompt the README recommends and the authors' evaluation script assembles: the background of the causal model the question was generated from, taken from `cladder-v1-meta-models.json`, then the question's given information, then the question, joined by single spaces. The text is reproduced as published. [README](https://github.com/causalNLP/cladder/blob/3d2d1169b4b939a09048a6a75956c8972a93cc38/README.md) and [evaluation script](https://github.com/causalNLP/cladder/blob/3d2d1169b4b939a09048a6a75956c8972a93cc38/causalbenchmark/eval/run_gpt_v1.5.py)

Each Solution starts with the answer, `yes` or `no`. For 8,532 questions it then gives the published derivation, one step per line: the variables, the graph's edges, the query's formal expression, the estimand, the probabilities used, the calculation, and the comparison that decides the answer. In the 158 collider-bias questions the step listing probabilities is empty upstream and shows as a blank line. The 1,580 questions about backdoor adjustment sets are published without a derivation, so their Solution is the answer alone.

Keys are the upstream question numbers, which run from 4 to 31019 with gaps. The archive has no per-question address, so source links point at the archive at the pinned commit. The importer uses only Python's standard library. It checks the archive's digest, the question count, that question numbers are unique, that the answers are balanced, that every question's causal model exists, and that every question other than the backdoor-adjustment ones has a derivation. It can be rerun with `python3 data/cladder/import.py`.
scoring:
CLadder is scored as accuracy: the fraction of questions answered correctly. The paper reports it overall, by rung, and by kind of story. Because half of the answers are yes, guessing scores about 50%. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04350)

The authors' evaluation script for this set asks the model to start its answer with "Yes" or "No" followed by its reasoning, and counts a response as yes or no when its lowercased text begins with that word; a response that begins with neither is wrong. The script also skips question numbers listed in a file that is not in the repository. [Evaluation script](https://github.com/causalNLP/cladder/blob/3d2d1169b4b939a09048a6a75956c8972a93cc38/causalbenchmark/eval/run_gpt_v1.5.py)

Benchopedia's runner sends each prompt with an instruction to end the reply with a line `Answer: yes` or `Answer: no`, reads that word, and compares it with the answer. Each task is tried five times and passes a run only when all five attempts pass, so guessing passes one time in 32.
limitations:
The language is generated from templates and reads that way. The authors measured 1.26 grammatical errors per 100 words. A graduate student who had taken causality courses judged 96% of 50 sampled questions readable, and an expert who answered a different sample of 50 got 82% right, so some questions are hard to read or to answer even for people trained in causal inference. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04350)

The questions are not independent. They were generated from 5,268 causal models, up to seven questions each, so questions from the same model share their background and probabilities. Within a story, questions also repeat templates, so the 10,112 questions cover far fewer distinct situations than their number suggests. The nonsense stories use made-up words, so those questions test reasoning over stated structure only.

The 1,580 backdoor-adjustment questions have no published derivation, so their Solutions show only the answer. The questions and answers have been public since 2023, and the dataset carries no canary string.
